titulo: A Million and a Half People
subtitulo: The Asia Minor Catastrophe, the 1923 population exchange, and the nation born of its own defeat (1919–1930)

coda.heading: Coda for the trip: what to look at

items.text: First, the names. Touring Athens you will see Nea Smyrni, Nea Ionia, Nea Filadelfia, Nea Erythraia. Each "Nea" is a city of Anatolia transplanted onto a neighborhood. It is the toponymy of mourning, and it is the same operation performed by Andean migrants when they named their Lima settlements after their towns of origin. In both cases, the peripheral city is a map of origins.

Second, the music. Seek out a night of live rebetiko — there are venues in Psyrri and Exarchia, and the crowd is mostly Greek, not tourists. Listen to the instrumentation and notice how the audience knows the lyrics by heart. You are hearing the cultural production of an uprooting a century old, and you will be doing exactly what you would do at a peña or a cumbia concert in Lima.

Third, at the Benaki Museum there are collections of costumes, textiles, and objects from the communities of Asia Minor and Pontus: what could be carried on a boat. It is the exact materiality of a displacement, and for a sociologist it is worth more than any explanatory panel.

Fourth, if the subject comes up in conversation, listen for whether someone says "my grandmother was from Smyrna" or "we are from Pontus." A hundred years later, refugee origin remains a piece of identity that gets transmitted and declared. Ask what was kept: recipes, words, nicknames, a devotion. It is an interview that conducts itself.

sections.heading: How to lose a war you were winning
paragraphs: In May 1919, Greek troops landed at Smyrna with authorization from the victorious powers of the First World War, who were dividing up the remains of the Ottoman Empire. The city had a large and prosperous Greek population; the landing was met with enthusiasm by them and with violence against the Muslim population from the very first hours. The Treaty of Sèvres, in 1920, assigned Greece administration of the Smyrna zone with a referendum planned for five years later. The Megali Idea seemed on the verge of being realized.

Three factors destroyed that prospect. The first: the Turkish nationalist movement led by Mustafa Kemal rejected Sèvres, organized an alternative government in Ankara, and turned the war into a struggle of national liberation, with the moral and logistical advantage that confers on one's own territory. The second: in November 1920, Venizelos lost the elections — an electorate exhausted by ten years of continuous war voted for peace — and King Constantine, the same man the Allies had deposed in 1917, returned to the throne. France and Italy used that return as a pretext to withdraw their support and seek their own arrangements with Ankara; Great Britain was left alone backing Greece, and half-heartedly. The third: the new government purged the Venizelist high command in the middle of the campaign and ordered an advance on Ankara that stretched supply lines to the breaking point.

The offensive stalled at the Sakarya River in August and September 1921, after weeks of fighting. A year of stalemate followed. In August 1922 the Turkish army attacked and the Greek front collapsed within days. The retreat was chaotic and accompanied by the destruction of villages. On September 9 Turkish troops entered Smyrna; a few days later the city burned — the Greek and Armenian quarters were destroyed, the Turkish and Jewish ones were not — and tens of thousands of people died or vanished as they crowded onto the quay. Allied warships anchored in the bay watched without intervening for days, under instructions of neutrality.
The overall figure for the disaster: around a million and a half people displaced, and a three-thousand-year Greek presence in Anatolia ended within a few weeks.

sections.heading: Lausanne 1923: ethnic cleansing as international treaty
paragraphs: The Treaty of Lausanne, in January and July 1923, contains a convention that deserves to be read with all possible coldness: the COMPULSORY POPULATION EXCHANGE between Greece and Turkey. It was not a consequence of the war: it was a diplomatic agreement, negotiated with mediation from the League of Nations and from the Norwegian Fridtjof Nansen, Nobel Peace laureate, which established the forced transfer and denationalization of approximately one million two hundred thousand Orthodox Christians from Anatolia to Greece, and of about four hundred thousand Muslims from Greece to Turkey. The Greeks of Istanbul and the Muslims of western Thrace were exempted.

The classifying criterion was the one we anticipated in installment 9: RELIGION, not language or self-consciousness. Thus the Karamanlides were deported to Greece — Orthodox Christians from Cappadocia who spoke only Turkish and wrote it in Greek characters — and Muslims from Crete who spoke only Greek, and whose descendants still speak it in some localities on the Turkish coast, were deported to Turkey. A premodern imperial criterion — the Ottoman millet — applied by two modern nation-states with international legal instruments.

And it was considered a success. For decades, the Greek-Turkish exchange was cited in the diplomatic literature as a precedent for resolving ethnic conflicts through orderly separation; it was invoked in discussions about central Europe in 1945 and about later conflicts. In other words: the model of forced homogenization enjoyed technical prestige. It is worth knowing this when discussing exactly what the international community considers acceptable in each era.

sections.heading: What the refugees did to Greece
paragraphs: The arrival of more than a million people into a country of about five million — a population increase of nearly a quarter within a few months, in an economy ruined by a decade of war — is one of the largest demographic shocks in European history. Entire neighborhoods sprang up on the outskirts of Athens, Piraeus, and Thessaloniki, whose names still announce their origin: Nea Ionia, Nea Smyrni, Nea Filadelfia, Kaisariani, Kokkinia. Agrarian reform accelerated in Macedonia, distributing among refugees the lands of the Muslims who had left: Greece became, almost by accident, a country of small agrarian proprietors, which in turn explains why it never had a peasant revolution.

The newcomers were, in many cases, urban, literate, and skilled, and they were arriving in a country poorer and more rural than the one they had left. Their integration was conflictive: the local population contemptuously called them TOURKOSPOROI, "Turk-seed," and that hostility pushed them politically toward Venizelos first and toward the left afterward. The refugee neighborhoods would become, twenty years later, the urban core of resistance against the occupation and of the civil war.

And they brought music. REBETIKO — songs of the urban margins, with bouzouki and baglamas, about prison, hashish, poverty, exile, and love — took shape in the refugee neighborhoods and the ports, was despised by the elites as the music of criminals, censored by the Metaxas dictatorship and by later governments, and ended up recognized as national heritage by UNESCO in 2017.

The Peruvian parallel here is exact, and I think it is one of the most productive in the whole plan. The forced displacement of the internal armed conflict between 1980 and 2000 expelled hundreds of thousands of people from the highlands toward Lima and intermediate cities; entire neighborhoods sprang up on the periphery; the newcomers were stigmatized; and they produced CHICHA and Andean cumbia, migrant music, despised by the Lima elite as vulgar, and today incorporated into the national cultural heritage and brand. Rebetiko and chicha are the same phenomenon: the culture of the displaced as the most vital aesthetic production of a society that rejected them. In both cases, moreover, that music was the vehicle through which the displaced became visible before they were recognized politically.

sections.heading: The paradox: the catastrophe produced the nation
paragraphs: Here is the central argument of this installment, and it is one worth holding onto with discomfort.

Before 1922, Greece was a state with a third of its new territories' population made up of minorities, and with an irredentist program that committed it to permanent war. After 1923, following the most complete defeat in its history, Greece became one of the most ethnically homogeneous states in Europe: the proportion of minorities fell dramatically. The MEGALI IDEA died in Smyrna, and with it the expansionist foreign policy that had ruined the country for eighty years.

In other words: the national project was realized through its own failure. The ethnic homogeneity that nationalist ideology considered desirable was produced by defeat, not victory, and at an atrocious human cost paid by populations that had decided nothing. That is the structural irony that organizes twentieth-century Greek history, and it also explains why 1922 is called "the Catastrophe" and not "the defeat": the word registers that what was lost was not a war but an entire world, that of the Greek communities of Anatolia, of Pontus, of Cappadocia, with their dialects and their customs, dissolved into mainland Greece within two generations.

Put in general terms: national homogenization projects do not fail for lack of will; rather, when they succeed, they do so by means their own ideology cannot acknowledge. Nationalism prefers to tell its origin story as an awakening, not as a deportation. It holds for Greece in 1923, for Turkey — whose republic is born in October 1923 through the same procedure, following the Armenian genocide of 1915 that was its direct precedent — and it holds as a way of thinking about how Peru narrates the formation of its own national population.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: the country of refugees that guards the border
paragraphs: The sharpest resonance is immediate and visible. Greece — a country where a very high share of the population descends from the refugees of 1923, with surnames, neighborhood nicknames, and recipes that record it — has since 2015 been the principal land and sea gateway for asylum seekers into the European Union. In 2015 and 2016 nearly a million people crossed via the Aegean islands; they keep arriving, in smaller but steady numbers, and European policy has drifted toward containment: the 2016 EU-Turkey agreement, the closed camps on the islands, and the documented practice of summary pushbacks in the Aegean and at the Evros River, denounced by European bodies and by journalistic investigations between 2020 and 2025, and always officially denied. The Pylos shipwreck of June 2023, with more than five hundred missing, is the gravest episode.

Greek society lives that tension visibly: there is widespread solidarity, with neighborhood networks and volunteering that in 2015 were exemplary and earned the country Nobel Peace Prize nominations, and there is simultaneously growing rejection on the most affected islands and a far-right party that capitalizes on it. That a nation built by refugees should today administer a border that produces deaths is not individual hypocrisy: it is the difference between family memory and reasons of state, and that difference is exactly what needs to be observed.

The Peruvian version lies in the response to Venezuelan migration since 2017 — more than a million and a half people, the region's second-largest reception — in a country whose own recent history is one of massive internal displacement. The sequence of initial welcome, deterioration of public discourse, media criminalization, tightening of requirements, and electoral use of the issue between 2021 and 2026 reproduces the Greek curve with remarkable fidelity. In both cases, the memory of one's own displacement vaccinated against nothing. That unpleasant finding is more useful than any appeal to historical empathy.
